title: Polenta Concia
subtitle: Alpine polenta with butter, Fontina, and Parmesan
excerpt: Polenta concia is the richest version of polenta: slow-cooked polenta stirred repeatedly with large amounts of butter and two cheeses until it is intensely creamy and savoury. Concia means dressed or seasoned. It is the celebratory polenta of the Aosta Valley and Alpine Piedmont.
sourceNotes: Polenta concia is the signature polenta of the Aosta Valley, where Fontina DOP cheese is produced. It is made by incorporating Fontina and butter into the polenta as it cooks, which gives it a richness far beyond plain polenta. The dish is also known as polenta taragna when buckwheat flour is added.

content.text: Polenta concia needs to be stirred often and patiently for 40 to 45 minutes. The cheese and butter are added in stages: some goes in during cooking and the rest at the finish. The result should be very rich and slightly stringy from the Fontina. It is a side dish or a main course, not a base for other sauces -- it needs nothing on top.

items.prepNote: rind removed, cut into small pieces

content.text: Bring 1.2 litres of water to a boil with {{salt-table}} salt. Pour in {{polenta}} polenta in a thin stream, stirring constantly. Reduce to a very low heat. Stir every few minutes with a wooden spoon.

After 20 minutes, add half the {{unsalted-butter}} butter and half the {{fontina}} Fontina. Stir well to melt. Continue cooking for another 20 to 25 minutes, stirring regularly, until the polenta is very thick and pulling away from the sides of the pan.

Remove from the heat. Stir in the remaining {{unsalted-butter}} butter, {{fontina}} Fontina, and {{parmesan}} Parmesan until melted and creamy. The polenta should be very rich and slightly stringy. Serve immediately in warm bowls.

items.symptom: The Fontina is not melting smoothly
items.cause: The polenta cooled slightly before the cheese was added.
items.fix: Add the cheese when the polenta is still very hot and off the heat. Stir vigorously -- Fontina melts into strings before it becomes smooth, which is normal and correct.

content.text: Polenta concia is the speciality of the Aosta Valley, a small Alpine region where Fontina DOP is produced. It is the polenta served at the end of a day on the mountain, designed to be warming and sustaining. The Aosta Valley version always uses Fontina; a related dish from Lombardy, polenta taragna, adds buckwheat flour to the polenta mix and uses a local cheese called scimudin. Both are among the richest preparations in the Italian Alpine tradition.
